title: Understanding APIs & Data Exchange
intro: Meet the digital waiter: see how an API carries your request to a server and brings back exactly the data you asked for, with no code needed.
recap: An API takes your request to a remote system and brings back only the data you asked for.
The client and the server follow agreed rules, like a contract.
Requests and responses travel as HTTP messages, and responses usually carry JSON.
Status codes such as 200, 401, 404 and 500 tell you what happened.

aiTutor.recap: Welcome to your first tutorial. This lesson explores how apps talk to each other across the internet without sharing their private inner workings. The waiter in the story is the idea to keep: a go-between who carries your request and brings back only what you asked for.
aiTutor.watchOut: An API is not the app, and it is not the database. It is the agreed doorway between them, which is why the kitchen in the story stays private.

glossary.definition: Application Programming Interface: a set of agreed rules that lets different software applications talk to each other.
glossary.example: When a ride-hailing app shows a live map, it uses a mapping service's API to ask for the map.

paragraphs: Imagine walking into a restaurant. You are the customer sitting at a table, and the kitchen is the system preparing your food. You cannot simply walk into the kitchen and cook the meal yourself—there are safety, security, and privacy boundaries.
Instead, a waiter comes to your table, takes your order to the kitchen, and brings back your meal. In the digital world, an API is that waiter.

The waiter works from a menu: it says what you can order and what you will get. An API has the same kind of agreement, called a contract. It is a set of rules for what an app may ask for, what it must send, and what it will get back. Because of the contract, the kitchen stays private, just as a company keeps its database (where it stores its records) private.

screens.title: From Your Phone to the Server

aiTutor.recap: This screen takes the waiter into real life. Your app sends a request, a server answers it, and the answer usually travels as small plain text.
aiTutor.example: You open a weather app and see today's forecast. The app did not measure the weather itself. It sent a request to a weather service's API and showed you the answer that came back.
aiTutor.tryThis: Pick an app on your phone that shows live information, such as maps, money or weather. Ask yourself what it must be asking for from somewhere else.

glossary.definition: A computer, often far away, that stores data or runs a service and answers requests from other devices.
glossary.example: The computer that answers your weather app's request is a server.

glossary.definition: A message from your app asking another system for something, such as data or an action.
glossary.example: "Give me today's forecast for Lagos" is a request.

paragraphs: Whenever you check the weather on your phone, send a mobile money transfer, or view a map inside a ride-hailing app, an API takes your app's request to a server (a computer somewhere else) and brings back the data you need.
The answer often comes back as JSON: short, plain text that holds only the data, such as the temperature, with no pictures or page design. That keeps it small and light on your mobile data.
You do not always need to write code to use one. No-code tools, such as Zapier and Make, connect apps this way, using simple visual steps.

aiTutor.explain: Think about what an API actually delivers. It does not hand over internal database passwords or raw source code. It provides an agreed contract: what you may ask for, what you must send, and what you will get back.
aiTutor.watchOut: A contract can be changed by the service that owns it. Apps that rely on an API sometimes need to update when the rules change.

widgetData.prompt: Complete the sentence about what an API does:
widgetData.template: An API works as an agreed {blank} that lets two apps share data without opening up their databases.
widgetData.explanation: An API is an agreed contract: what you can ask for, what you must send, and what the reply looks like. Each side only has to follow the contract, so neither needs to see how the other works inside.
widgetData.bonusFact: Because the contract stays the same while the inside changes, a company can rebuild its systems without breaking the apps that depend on it.

aiTutor.explain: Consider weather or navigation apps. Ride-hailing companies do not launch their own mapping satellites; they use external APIs to ask for maps. Picking the answer is about who holds the data, and who asks for it.
aiTutor.watchOut: Do not pick the answer that says the data is copied into the app. Live information, such as traffic, has to be asked for each time.

widgetData.question: When you book a ride on an app and see a live map, how does that app display Google Maps?

options.text: The app developers copied all of Google's satellite photos directly into the app file.
The app sends an API request with your coordinates to Google Maps, which returns the map tiles.
Your smartphone hardware renders satellite imagery locally without an internet connection.

widgetData.explanation: The ride-hailing app connects to a mapping service's API and requests the map tiles it needs as you move, instead of storing the whole world's imagery.
widgetData.bonusFact: APIs let small teams build products quickly by combining services that others already run, such as maps, payments and messaging.

aiTutor.explain: Decide whether each statement is true or false to test your intuition about how APIs behave. Think about the waiter: a go-between that checks, carries and returns, without giving away the kitchen.
aiTutor.tryThis: For each card, picture the restaurant story. Which part of the story does the card describe?

widgetData.instruction: Evaluate each card as True or False:

cards.statement: An API allows you to access external data without having direct access to the remote database.
cards.explanation: The API acts as a guard. It checks your permission before any request reaches the database, so you only see what you are allowed to see.
cards.bonusFact: This is why an app can show your balance without ever having a copy of the bank's database.

cards.statement: You must write computer code to get any use out of an API.
cards.explanation: No-code automation tools such as Zapier, Make and Airtable connect services through their APIs using visual steps, so many useful connections need no programming.
cards.bonusFact: If you can describe a connection as "when this happens, do that", a no-code tool can probably build it.

cards.statement: An API often sends back small, plain text (JSON), not a full web page.
cards.explanation: JSON is compact, readable text that carries just the data, not a full web page with pictures and layout. That keeps responses small and quick on a phone.
cards.bonusFact: Smaller responses use less mobile data, which matters when data is expensive.

aiTutor.explain: Tap each of the three steps in the lifecycle below to learn how an API transaction completes. Request goes out, the server works, and a response comes back. Almost every API call follows this shape.
aiTutor.example: You tap "check balance". The app sends a request, the bank's server confirms who you are and looks up the amount, and the response carries the balance and a 200 OK status.
aiTutor.watchOut: If any step fails, the whole call fails. A request with a missing key is stopped at the server, and a broken server cannot answer at all.
aiTutor.tryThis: Next time an app shows an error, ask which of the three steps it probably failed at.

walkThrough.title: Checking your balance, one request at a time
steps: You tap "check balance" in your banking app. The app is the client.
Request: the app sends a message to the bank's server with your account details and a security token.
Server logic: the server checks the token, confirms the request is allowed, and looks up your balance.
Response: the server sends back a 200 OK status and your balance as a small piece of JSON.
The app turns that JSON into the number on your screen. At no point did the app see the bank's database.

nodes.label: 1. Request
nodes.title: HTTP Request
nodes.definition: Your app (the client) sends a message saying what it wants. It includes the service's web address, the kind of action (GET to fetch something, POST to send something new), and often a key (a secret code that identifies the app) or your login.
nodes.bonusFact: HTTP is the set of rules the web uses to send these messages.

nodes.label: 2. Server Processing
nodes.title: Server Logic & Auth
nodes.definition: The server checks who is asking, limits how many requests can come in a short time, looks up the data and prepares the answer.
nodes.bonusFact: Limiting requests protects a server from being overwhelmed when thousands arrive at once.

nodes.label: 3. Response
nodes.title: HTTP Response
nodes.definition: The server sends back a status code, a short number that says what happened, usually with the data. 200 OK: it worked. 401 Unauthorized: the key or login is missing. 404 Not Found: what you asked for does not exist. 500 Server Error: the server itself failed.
nodes.bonusFact: If something went wrong, the response provides an error message explaining why.

widgetData.completionMessage: You've explored every step of the request-response lifecycle.
widgetData.completionBonusFact: Understanding this three-part cycle makes sense of errors like 404 and 500 much faster. The code tells you which side to look at first.

aiTutor.review: Almost done. Match each standard status code with its real-world outcome to complete this tutorial. The first digit is a good clue: 2 means success, 4 means the request had a problem, and 5 means the server had one.
aiTutor.example: You open a page that has been removed and see 404. The server worked fine; it simply has nothing at that address.
aiTutor.watchOut: 401 and 404 can look alike on screen, but they mean different things. 401 means you are not allowed in, 404 means there is nothing there to open.

widgetData.instruction: Match each HTTP status code with its meaning:

pairs.right: Request succeeded and data was returned
API key or user login is missing
The requested endpoint does not exist
The remote server crashed or failed internally

widgetData.explanation: Standardized status codes let developers immediately recognize whether a request succeeded (200), was blocked (401), missed (404), or broke the server (500).
widgetData.bonusFact: Status codes are an agreed web standard, so apps built by different teams read a 404 the same way.
